lessons.title: Principles of organisation
lessons.summary: See how cells are organised into tissues, organs and organ systems, and use the stomach and the digestive system as worked examples of each level.
objectives: I can describe the levels of organisation from cells to organisms.
I can define a tissue, an organ and an organ system and give examples of each.
I can explain how the stomach is made from several different tissues working together.
I can place structures in the correct level of organisation.

activities.title: Building a body from cells
activities.content:
## From cells to organisms

A human body contains trillions of cells, but they are not simply piled up at random. Living things are built in **levels of organisation**, with each level made from the one below it:

```
cell -> tissue -> organ -> organ system -> organism
```

- A **cell** is the basic building block of all living things. Many cells are **specialised**, meaning their structure suits one particular job.
- A **tissue** is a group of similar cells working together to carry out a shared function.
- An **organ** is a group of different tissues working together to carry out a particular function.
- An **organ system** is a group of organs working together to carry out a major job for the body.
- An **organism** is a complete living thing made of several organ systems.

This pattern is the same in plants and in animals. The key idea to remember is that each level is built from *groups* of the level beneath. A tissue is not one cell, and an organ is not one tissue.

activities.title: Worked example: sorting structures into levels
activities.content:
**Where does each structure belong?**

| Structure | Level | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Red blood cell | Cell | A single specialised unit |
| Muscle tissue | Tissue | Many similar muscle cells contracting together |
| Heart | Organ | Muscle, nervous and connective tissues working together to pump blood |
| Circulatory system | Organ system | Heart, blood vessels and blood working together |
| A dog | Organism | Made of many organ systems |

**Common mix-up:** students often call blood a *cell*. Blood is actually a **tissue**, because it is a collection of cells (red cells, white cells, platelets) in plasma, all working together to transport substances.

question.text: Put these levels of organisation in order from smallest to largest.
question.hint: Start with the single building block and finish with the whole living thing.
question.explanation: Cells group into tissues, tissues into organs, organs into organ systems, and organ systems make up an organism.

activities.title: Tissues: teams of similar cells
activities.content:
## What makes a tissue?

A tissue is a group of cells that have a **similar structure** and a **shared function**. Three tissues you must be able to name are found in the stomach:

- **Muscular tissue** is made of cells that can shorten (contract). In the stomach, the muscular tissue contracts to churn food and mix it with digestive juices.
- **Glandular tissue** is made of cells that make and release (secrete) useful substances. In the stomach, the glandular tissue produces **digestive juices** containing enzymes and hydrochloric acid.
- **Epithelial tissue** is a thin covering layer. It lines the inside and outside of the stomach and protects the layers underneath.

Other tissues include **nervous tissue** (carries electrical signals), **connective tissue** (holds structures together) and, in plants, tissues such as **xylem** and **phloem**.

Notice that each tissue has one main job. A tissue on its own cannot digest a meal or pump blood. Only when several tissues are combined does an organ appear that can do a complete task.

activities.title: Worked example: the stomach as an organ
activities.content:
**The stomach is an organ. Explain why, using named tissues.**

A good answer links the definition to the example:

1. An organ is a group of *different* tissues working together for one function.
2. The stomach contains **muscular tissue** that contracts to churn the contents.
3. It contains **glandular tissue** that secretes digestive juices.
4. It contains **epithelial tissue** that covers and lines it.
5. Together these tissues carry out the stomach's function: **breaking down food** physically and chemically.

The important word is *different*. If the stomach were made of only one kind of tissue it would still be a tissue, not an organ.

question.text: Match each stomach tissue to its role.
question.hint: Think about which tissue moves, which one makes substances, and which one covers.
question.explanation: Muscular tissue contracts to churn food; glandular tissue secretes digestive juices; epithelial tissue lines and protects the stomach.

pairs.right: Covers the inside and outside of the stomach

question.text: Which statement correctly describes an organ?
question.explanation: An organ is a group of different tissues working together to perform a function, such as the heart or the stomach.

options.text: A group of different tissues working together to perform a particular function
A group of similar cells working together to perform a particular function
options.feedback: That is the definition of a tissue.

options.text: A group of organs working together to perform a major function
A single specialised cell with one job

activities.title: Organ systems and organisms
activities.content:
## Organ systems

An **organ system** is a group of organs that together carry out one of the body's major jobs. Examples:

| Organ system | Some organs it contains | Main job |
|---|---|---|
| Digestive system | Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, liver, pancreas | Breaks food into small soluble molecules and absorbs them |
| Circulatory system | Heart, arteries, veins, capillaries | Transports substances around the body |
| Respiratory system | Trachea, bronchi, lungs | Gets oxygen into the blood and carbon dioxide out |
| Nervous system | Brain, spinal cord, nerves | Detects changes and coordinates responses |

The organs in a system do not have to be next to each other. The liver and pancreas are part of the digestive system even though food never passes through them, because they make substances (bile and enzymes) that are released into the gut.

All of the organ systems together make up the **organism**. In a multicellular organism, the systems depend on one another: the digestive system supplies glucose, the respiratory system supplies oxygen, and the circulatory system delivers both to every cell.

question.text: Which of the following are organs of the digestive system? Select all that apply.
question.hint: Some digestive organs release substances into the gut without food passing through them.
question.explanation: The pancreas and the small intestine are digestive organs. The heart belongs to the circulatory system and the lungs to the respiratory system.

options.feedback: The heart is part of the circulatory system.
The lungs belong to the respiratory system.

metadata.blanksText: A tissue is a group of ___ cells working together, whereas an organ is a group of different ___ working together.

question.hint: Tissues are made from cells that look alike; organs are made from more than one type of the next level up.
question.explanation: A tissue is a group of similar cells with a shared function. An organ is a group of different tissues working together.

question.text:
The stomach is described as an organ.

(a) Define the term *organ*. (1 mark)

(b) Name **two** tissues found in the stomach and describe the function of each. (2 marks)

(c) Name the organ system that the stomach belongs to. (1 mark)
question.hint: For (b), choose tissues with clearly different jobs: one that moves, one that makes substances, or one that covers.
question.explanation: (a) An organ is a group of different tissues working together to carry out a particular function. (b) Muscular tissue contracts to churn the food; glandular tissue secretes digestive juices (enzymes and acid); epithelial tissue covers and lines the stomach. (c) The digestive system.

markScheme.criterion: Organ defined as a group of different tissues working together for a function
Muscular tissue named and its function (contracts/churns food) given
Glandular or epithelial tissue named with correct function (secretes digestive juice / covers and protects)

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- Living things are organised in levels: **cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism**.
- A **tissue** is a group of *similar* cells with a shared function (e.g. muscular, glandular, epithelial).
- An **organ** is a group of *different* tissues working together (e.g. the stomach, the heart).
- An **organ system** is a group of organs working together (e.g. the digestive system).
- The stomach shows all three tissues: muscular tissue churns, glandular tissue secretes digestive juices, epithelial tissue lines and protects.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: blood is an organ.
practiceQuestions.hint: Blood is a collection of similar cells in a liquid, all doing transport jobs.
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. Blood is a tissue: a group of cells (red cells, white cells, platelets) in plasma, working together to transport substances.

practiceQuestions.text: Which of these is an example of an organ system?
practiceQuestions.hint: Look for a group of several organs.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The circulatory system is an organ system made of the heart, blood vessels and blood. The others are an organ, a tissue and a cell.

options.feedback: The heart is a single organ.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentence about the stomach.

metadata.blanksText: In the stomach, ___ tissue produces digestive juices, while ___ tissue contracts to churn the food.

practiceQuestions.hint: One tissue is named after glands; the other is named after muscles.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Glandular tissue secretes digestive juices; muscular tissue contracts to churn the contents.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each example to its level of organisation.
practiceQuestions.hint: Ask: is it one unit, a group of similar cells, a group of tissues, or a group of organs?
practiceQuestions.explanation: A sperm cell is a cell; xylem is a tissue; a leaf is an organ; the respiratory system is an organ system.

practiceQuestions.text: Which statements about tissues are correct? Select all that apply.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about the definition: similar cells, shared function.
practiceQuestions.explanation: A tissue is a group of similar cells with a shared function, and epithelial tissue is a real example. Tissues are smaller than organs, and organs contain more than one tissue.

options.text: A tissue is a group of similar cells with a shared function
Epithelial tissue covers surfaces of organs
A tissue is larger than an organ
options.feedback: Organs are made of tissues, so they are larger.

options.text: Each organ is made of only one tissue

practiceQuestions.text: Explain why the heart is classed as an organ rather than a tissue.
practiceQuestions.hint: Use the definition of an organ and name at least one tissue in the heart.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The heart contains several different tissues (for example muscular tissue that contracts, nervous tissue that controls the rhythm, and connective tissue) that work together to pump blood. A tissue contains only one type of cell.

markScheme.criterion: States that the heart is made of several different tissues
States that the tissues work together to carry out a function (pumping blood)

practiceQuestions.text: Arrange these structures from the digestive system in order from smallest to largest level of organisation.
practiceQuestions.hint: One of these is the whole system; one is a single cell.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Epithelial cell (cell) → glandular tissue (tissue) → stomach (organ) → digestive system (organ system).

practiceQuestions.text: The pancreas does not have food passing through it, yet it is part of the digestive system. Why?
practiceQuestions.hint: What does the pancreas release, and where does it go?
practiceQuestions.explanation: The pancreas produces digestive enzymes that are released into the small intestine, so it contributes to the function of the digestive system.

options.text: It produces enzymes that are released into the gut to digest food
It absorbs digested food into the blood
options.feedback: Absorption happens in the small intestine.

options.text: It pumps blood to the stomach

practiceQuestions.text:
A student looks at a thin slice of a leaf under a microscope and sees several layers of different-looking cells.

(a) Explain why the leaf is described as an organ. (2 marks)

(b) The student says: "Each layer of cells in the leaf is an organ system." Explain why the student is wrong and state the correct term for a single layer of similar cells. (2 marks)
practiceQuestions.hint: For (b), a single layer of similar cells is a level *below* an organ.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) The leaf contains several different tissues (for example epidermal tissue, palisade mesophyll, spongy mesophyll, xylem and phloem) that work together to carry out photosynthesis. (b) An organ system is a group of organs, which is a level above an organ. A single layer of similar cells with one function is a tissue.

markScheme.criterion: Tissues work together to carry out a function such as photosynthesis
Organ system is a group of organs / a level above an organ
A layer of similar cells is a tissue

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: plants are organised into tissues, organs and organ systems in the same way as animals.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about roots, stems and leaves.
practiceQuestions.explanation: True. Plants have tissues (such as xylem and phloem), organs (such as leaves and roots) and organ systems (such as the transport system).
